<reason>Side B (PRO) won a close, well-matched debate. Both sides answered pressure questions directly with A1/A2 structure and kept the clash narrow. A's strongest surviving points were the insider-exposure risk of secure rooms for vulnerable teens and the "societal impact as viewpoint judgment" objection to accreditation. But B consistently out-weighed: the two-tier answer (secure rooms for rare trajectories, DP for exports) blunted the noise dilemma; the IRB/statistical-agency analogy gave a working institutional precedent A never fully dismantled; and B's asymmetry frame — CON demands perfection from public science while accepting unaudited commercial exploitation — went largely unanswered. Critically, B's closing "you cannot restrict what you cannot measure" directly damaged A's alternative of blind direct regulation and subpoena-based investigation, and A never repaired it. A's rhetoric was vivid and grounded, with no fake precision on either side, but B made the debate easier to decide and left more live routes standing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.1-B4.2's tiered-access answer to A's rare-trajectory dilemma, combined with B5.2's "you cannot restrict what you cannot measure" against A's regulation-instead-of-access alternative. A's best counter was A4.3's "noise only polices what leaves the room," which kept the secure-room exposure point alive, but B's institutional precedent and asymmetry weighing ultimately controlled the exchange.</best_rebuttal>
